how-much-to-charge-to-build-a-pole-barn..text:
← Pole barn bid calculator

How much to charge to build a pole barn

Post-frame shops get shopped on a published $45 a square foot or $28,000 for a 30×40 Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the eave or the floor. A 10-foot ag shell on gravel with two walk doors is a different job from a 16-foot shop with two overhead doors, a lean-to, a 6-inch slab, and a shop panel.

Open the free pole barn bid calculator

Price bays and extra eave, not square feet

A pole barn is posts and trusses on a spacing, then wall and roof steel. Divide the eave length by the post spacing and round up. A 40-foot building on 8-foot centers is five bays, fourteen posts, and six trusses. Each foot of eave above the included 10-foot coupon adds about 8 percent to frame and wall-steel hours — longer posts, more sheet, and more ladder time. A 16-foot shop is not a 10-foot barn with taller walls sketched on.

The floor is usually the job

Gravel is a spread. A 4-inch slab is ready-mix, rebar, and a crew day. A 6-inch reinforced slab is more yards and more steel. Matching a gravel per-foot special on a shop slab is how a sold barn becomes a two-week loss after the first concrete ticket.

Doors, lean-to, insulation, and a shop panel are not in the coupon

Walk doors are a half-hour each. An overhead door is a framed opening plus the door. A lean-to is extra posts, extra roof, and extra floor. Insulation and a 100-amp shop panel are their own tickets. The calculator prices the same barn three ways — gravel, 4-inch slab, 6-inch reinforced — so you can see which floor still keeps the margin when the owner asks you to “just match the other guy.”

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the pole barn bid calculator. It is not a structural specification, an engineered stamp, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to build a pole barn?

Charge from bay count, eave height, doors, lean-to, and the floor — not a published per-square-foot special. A 30×40×10 ag shell on gravel with two walk doors is a different job from a 40×60×16 shop with two overhead doors, a lean-to, and a 6-inch slab.

How many posts does a pole barn need?

Divide the eave length by the post spacing and round up to get bays. Posts sit at both ends of every bay on both eaves, plus two extra gable posts that are not the shared corners. A 40-foot building on 8-foot centers is 5 bays, 12 eave posts, and 2 gable posts.

Does eave height change a pole barn bid?

Yes. Each foot above the included 10-foot coupon adds about 8 percent to frame and wall-steel hours — longer posts, more sheet, and more ladder time. A 16-foot shop is not a 10-foot ag barn with taller walls sketched on.

Why is a gravel-floor barn cheaper than a slab shop?

Gravel is a spread. A 4-inch slab is ready-mix, rebar, and a crew day. A 6-inch reinforced slab is more yards and more steel. Matching a gravel per-foot special on a shop slab is how a sold barn becomes a two-week loss after the first concrete ticket.

vs-a-flat-price-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Pole Barn Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per square foot

“$X a square foot” or “$28,000 for a 30×40” is not a price for a pole barn — it is a price for one specific eave height, floor, and door count, quietly applied to every building that calls in.

What a flat price per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a post-frame building: multiply the footprint by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a Facebook special or a competitor's flyer will call and ask you to match, whatever their building actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — a shallow ag shell on gravel, no slab, no doors past a couple of walk-ins, no insulation, no shop electrical — and then reused for every barn afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the building's length, width, eave height, roof pitch, post spacing, floor (gravel, a 4-inch slab, or a 6-inch reinforced slab), insulation, an electrical package up to a shop panel, overhead and walk doors, a lean-to, and wainscot, plus your own labor hours and material costs. It prices the eave height, the floor, the doors, and every extra separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this building, not a generic one.

What a flat price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft at a 10-foot eave and a 16-foot eave, even though every foot above the base coupon height adds ladder work, longer posts, and an extra sheet of steel. Prices extra eave height separately as a factor on frame hours, so a taller building costs more than a shorter one of the same footprint.
Has no line for the floor, regardless of whether the building sits on bare gravel or a 6-inch reinforced slab with rebar. Prices floor hours, cubic yards, and rebar separately by floor kind, so a slab shop costs more than a gravel shell.
Has no line for overhead doors, walk doors, insulation, a shop electrical panel, or a lean-to, regardless of how many the job needs. Prices each extra separately — doors, insulation, electrical, and lean-to square footage — so a fully loaded shop costs more than a bare ag shell.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-square-foot rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two barns, the same footprint-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates ($28/hr crew wage, 28% burden, 15% overhead, a 20% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $15.59/sq ft rateGap
30×40×10 ag shell, gravel, 2 walk doors, no insulation, no electrical — 1,200 sq ft, the job the rate is set from$18,711.66 bid price; $14,969.33 break-even cost$18,711.66 (exactly $15.59/sq ft — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
40×60×16 commercial shop, 6" slab, 2 overhead doors, full insulation, a shop panel, 12-ft lean-to — 2,400 sq ft main building plus a 720 sq ft lean-to the rate never counts$101,933.52 bid price; $81,546.81 break-even cost$37,423.32The rate quotes $44,123.49 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $64,510.19 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $15.59/sq ft rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the ag-shell preset, divided by that preset's footprint. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the taller, slabbed, fully loaded shop, it prices only the 2,400 sq ft main footprint and never sees the lean-to, the slab, the doors, the insulation, or the shop panel at all. Run your own building's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-square-foot rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one building it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a pole barn bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is eave height, floor (gravel, a 4-inch slab, or a 6-inch reinforced slab), overhead and walk doors, insulation, a shop electrical panel, and a lean-to -- not square footage. A 40x60x16 commercial shop on a 6-inch slab with two overhead doors, full insulation, a shop panel, and a 12-foot lean-to is doing several jobs a 30x40x10 ag shell on gravel with two walk doors never touches, none of which scale with floor area the way a per-square-foot rate assumes.

What does a flat price per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Eave height above the base coupon height, the floor type (gravel versus a 4-inch or 6-inch slab), overhead doors, walk doors, a lean-to, wall or ceiling insulation, and a shop electrical panel. A 10-foot gravel shell with two walk doors is doing far less than a 16-foot shop with a slab, two overheads, insulation, a shop panel, and a lean-to -- and a per-square-foot number has no line for any of it.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped presets, at its own shipped shop rates: a 30x40x10 ag shell on gravel with two walk doors -- 1,200 sq ft -- prices at $18,711.66, or $15.59 a square foot. Applying that same $15.59 rate to a 40x60x16 commercial shop's 2,400 sq ft footprint (six-inch slab, two overhead doors, full insulation, a shop panel, and a 12-foot lean-to, which a per-square-foot number never counts at all) quotes $37,423.32 -- $44,123.49 below that job's own $81,546.81 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $64,510.19 below the calculator's own $101,933.52 bid price.

Is a flat price per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same eave height, same floor, no slab, no shop electrical, no lean-to -- a per-square-foot rate can land close, and on this calculator's own shallow ag-shell preset it is exactly the rate the job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which barn it was built on and neither does the estimator until eave height, floor, doors, insulation, and a lean-to are actually spelled out.

Does this calculator know what materials or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes the building's dimensions, eave height, roof pitch, floor, insulation, electrical, overhead and walk doors, and a lean-to, plus the labor hours and material costs you enter, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. JobTread

Two different shapes: JobTread is account-based project-management and job-costing software for running a home-building or remodeling business across clients, crews, and jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this pole barn cost, given its bays, eave, doors, and floor, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

JobTread is project-management and job-costing software marketed to residential home builders and remodelers, including post-frame and pole-barn shops. It is used to run budgets and estimates, a client communication portal, scheduling, purchase orders and change orders, and job costing across a whole company's pipeline, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job. JobTread's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — construction project-management and job-costing software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for JobTread appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what JobTread does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, track purchase orders, or run job costing across a pipeline, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes building length and width, post spacing, eave height, roof pitch, overhead and walk door counts, a lean-to, wainscot, insulation, electrical, and a gravel, 4-inch, or 6-inch slab floor, plus loaded wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, the recommended price to quote, and a copyable bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block.
